scope: Material-production comparison among Hodgson-described Nepali handmade paper, Darjeeling/Calcutta/Serampore experimental interfaces, British paper, East India Company-associated paper and wider European handmade paper. Geographic labels are not treated as secure production origins without independent evidence.
central_claim: Paper properties are produced by fibre, preparation, sheet-formation interface, finishing, transport/storage history and intended operation; geographic or fibre provenance alone is insufficient.
formula: paper_properties = fibre × preparation × sheet_formation_interface × finishing × transport_storage_history × intended_operation

regimes.label: Hodgson-described Nipalese/Nepali handmade paper system
regimes.production_origin_warning: Hodgson explicitly says the paper is not principally made in Nepal proper; Nepal/Kathmandu is a major market name and node.
regimes.raw_material: inner bark of Himalayan paper plant
regimes.mechanical_preparation: beating to homogeneous pulp; dilution/churning; coarse screening
regimes.sheet_formation: floating wooden frame with cloth bottom; manual distribution
regimes.thickness_control: pulp layer varied according to required strength
regimes.drying: frame set near large fire; sheet peeled after drying
regimes.finishing: optional polishing/burnishing with conch shell or hardwood
regimes.sizing: Hodgson reports no routine sizing required to prevent ink running

regimes.label: British remanufacture of transported Nepal pulp
regimes.input: dried Nepal paper pulp made into transport bricks
regimes.operation: British papermakers reprocess/bleach/form paper from transported pulp
regimes.bleaching_warning: Searchable 1833 scan reports unusually high chloride-of-lime/acid demand and probable texture injury; exact quantities require image verification before quotation.
regimes.control: Finished thin sheets made in Nepal and sent to Britain in 1829 were described as exceedingly tough and flexible and capable of taking minute bank-note plate impression with perfect fidelity.
regimes.interpretation: The same broad Himalayan material source did not reproduce local sheet properties under British remanufacture.
regimes.primary_source: JASB 2 (1833), Asiatic Society proceedings p.93, G. Swinton / Robison / Charles Cowan correspondence

regimes.label: Darjeeling reconstruction of Nepali papermaking
observed_process_corrections: flat stone and double-headed mallets used
iron boiler rejected because it darkened paper
continuous water flow used to remove alkali
regimes.interpretation: Embodied skill and local process calibration exceeded the portable printed recipe.
regimes.primary_source: Journal of the Agricultural and Horticultural Society of India 1 (1842), 210-221

regimes.label: Calcutta as paper evaluation, procurement and distribution hub
regimes.production_origin_class: not a single paper manufacture class
regimes.coding_rule: manufacture_place, purchase_place, test_place, print_place and administrative_destination must remain separate fields.

regimes.label: Serampore mechanised paper interface
regimes.historical_context: Government of India CPPRI identifies Serampore, West Bengal, as the site of India's first mechanised paper mill, established in 1812.
regimes.Hodgson_linked_operation: O'Shaughnessy bleaching result handed to Marshman at Serampore Paper Mills for practical larger-scale testing of Himalayan bark material.
regimes.failure: mucilaginous pulp impeded free flow on machine web and thickness control; economic/general quality concerns remained.
regimes.interpretation: A property bundle compatible with tough hand-sheet formation became a defect at the machine-web interface.

regimes.label: British handmade laid/wove rag paper
technical_context: Whatman wove mould from mid-18th century
regimes.source: British Association of Paper Historians, History of Papermaking in the UK

regimes.label: British early machine paper
regimes.historical_limit: best handmade grades continued where quality/durability/special use mattered

regimes.label: East India Company-associated British paper and Whatman supply context
regimes.supply_context: Secondary scholarship citing Balston reports the EIC as a major Whatman customer and an explicit aim to make papers able to stand Indian climates, replacing earlier Dutch Company supply.
object_comparators: Rylands Persian MS 922 endpaper: EIC insignia + countermark J. Whatman 1811; English handmade laid paper, approx. 9 laid lines/cm and 23 mm chain spacing
Rylands Persian MS 795 endpaper: heart-shaped EIC insignia dated 1820 + countermark J Whatman Balston & Co. 1820
source_control: EIC/VEIC watermark alone does not identify Whatman
J WHATMAN alone does not prove Turkey Mill/Whatman production

regimes.label: Dutch and wider European handmade paper market
dutch_characteristics: strong sizing identified as a quality factor
trade_context: French paper continued in lower-cost grades
British market itself supplemented domestic production with continental imports
wove technology crossed from Britain into Dutch production around 1807
regimes.whatman_imitation: Whatman marks were imitated/forged in France, Germany and Austria in the first half of the nineteenth century.
regimes.interpretation: European paper is a plural market of makers, technologies, grades and copied brands rather than one material class.

source_control_rules: Do not code Calcutta as manufacture origin from purchase, receipt, testing, printing or transit evidence.
Do not code historical 'Nipalese/Nepali paper' as made in Nepal proper without production-location evidence.
Do not code Whatman from imported status, whiteness, wove appearance, EIC context or Company watermark alone.
Do not use watermark alone when countermark, date, formation structure and maker chronology can be checked.
Exact chemical quantities in the 1833 British bleaching report require page-image verification before publication quotation.
